By telling a story.

are hard wired to understand.
Listen more carefully to a story.
A story is just a conversation you had with one person about a problem, where you were the setting,
how it was resolved, how you felt and what was learned from it.
That's all the story is.
Doesn't have to be funny, doesn't have to be dramatic.
You don't have to bring tears to people's eyes or your own eyes.
The best source of stories is just recounting an actual conversation you had about a problem with a
colleague, a co-worker, a client, a customer, a boss.
It's the ultimate example.
You've isolated the five key messages you have in your presentation.

Now, if you don't have a story from a message point, what that really means is you've never talked
to another human being about this message.
If that's the case, you've got to ask yourself, is this really an important.
Message, if there are no stories, typically that means it's not a very important message.

=== How to Deliver a Ceremonial Speech ===


--- Never Spotlight Your Blunders and Mistakes Again ---

The biggest moment for a lot of people when it comes to their body language in the workplace is when
they screw up.
Now we're all human beings.
We all make mistakes, and it's natural to be embarrassed.
The problem is, if you're giving any sort of speech, presentation, talk, a briefing and the people
don't really know you that much and you're going through serious business matters, it's that look of
that awkwardness, that embarrassment.
It becomes the most emotional moment of the whole talk, the whole presentation, the whole time when
they're experiencing it, it becomes the most memorable part.
That's a problem.
Now, it may generate sympathy, but that's not the main emotion we want to be getting out of our coworkers,
colleagues and clients.
We want them focused on how we can help them work with them, be an asset to them.
So I want to give you some tips.
For example, in the last video, I messed up.
I screwed up.
You may remember or you may not.
I went to grab my earpiece.
To make a point, I couldn't find it, I looked around, it was on the floor, I bent down and I picked
it up, so I made a mistake, hey, I'm human.
But here's what I didn't do.
I didn't go, oh, my God, where it is it?
Oh, I'm so sorry.
I didn't stop and spotlight it.
In my experience, it's never the mistakes people make in business presentations, meetings, talks,
briefings.
It's their reaction to their mistakes.
That's what gets people into trouble and unfortunately can even destroy careers.
Those of you who follow United States politics may remember there was a time a couple of political seasons
ago when the governor of Texas was running for president and he at that time was the front runner.
He was asked a question, what government agencies would he cut?
And he said, I will cut the following four agencies.
I will cut the Department of Energy, the Department of Commerce, the Environmental Protection Agency,
and that, uh uh.
Oh, uh.

And I would submit to you it wasn't because he forgot something.
It was his body language.
It was his voice.
It was the sense of, oh, I feel so awful, so embarrassed you caught me.
I feel like it was such a powerful moment that it became the most memorable thing anyone could remember
about him.
And that was the big problem.
Now, contrast, four years later, there was another politician from Texas running a senator.

And he listed three of them and he repeated one.

By that time, no one had formed any negative impressions based on that answer.

And he ended up coming in first place, but he did get second place so that campaign performance didn't
hurt him at all.
So the real lesson here is not that we have to be on all the time and be perfect.

not people you work with every single day and you're really close with in the workplace.

Don't act embarrassed.
Don't start apologizing.
Just do what I did.
You need a couple of seconds.
Pick up what you need.
Keep going.

If they do remember, it's not the dominant memory.
So remember, it's not your mistakes that get you into trouble.
It's typically your body language, your vocal change, reactions to your mistakes, showing embarrassment,
learn to control that and your mistakes really won't cut against you.

--- Eliminating Speaking Anxiety ---

If you have a fear of public speaking, relax, it just means your normal.
Most people have a fear of public speaking.
In fact, numerous polls have shown that the number one fear people have is public speaking.
So it's actually kind of weird if you don't fear public speaking, as Jerry Seinfeld always points out
because of this poll, it means most people, if they had to go to a funeral, would rather be in the
casket than delivering the eulogy.
Now, I think that is going too far.
I think most people, if you said, all right, you have to jump out of this plane without a parachute
or jump off this cliff or give a short speech, most people would be very happy to give that speech.
But I do think that giving a speech is one of those things that the average person could be asked to
do in the course of a normal week is the thing that creates a lot of tension that makes them uncomfortable.
So I do understand why people say they fear public speaking.
But I've got a little test for you right now.
If I say to you, you're going to go to a restaurant tonight and see your three best friends, it's
going to be a noisy, crowded restaurant.
There will be a lot of people around.
And you're going to talk to your best friends about the game you all saw last night that you care about
or a particular movie you all saw in the last week.
And everyone's passionate about it.
And now it's your turn to talk about what you thought of it.
And you've got a glass of wine or whatever you enjoy.
Now, are you nervous when you're talking?
Chances are no.
Well, guess what?
That's public speaking.
You're in a room.
There are a lot of people there and your mouth is moving.
You're speaking.
You guys sit.
Well, T.J., that's different.
Relaxed with friends.
It really isn't different.
The reason you're comfortable is, you know, how you're coming across.
You're feeling relaxed.
But the fact that there's a room full of people and your mouth is moving and sound is coming, that's
not actually making you nervous.
But you are doing public speaking now.
Why do I point that out?
It's because I believe most people who are nervous about public speaking are nervous in a narrower context.
They're nervous about speaking in public, in school or in business where they're not quite sure how
they're coming across and they're not quite sure if the information they're presenting is interesting
to anyone or is understandable to anyone.
If you're talking about the big game last night that you saw and you saw it with your buddies or your
friends, you know, they understand what you're talking about.
There's that sense of commonality.
And yet if you're giving a new business pitch, if you're talking to an angel investor or a venture
capitalist about why this person should fund your organization for a million dollars, you may be feeling

Why are we nervous when we speak?
Evolutionary biologists believe that human beings are programmed to fear being separated from the crowd.
It's a defense mechanism.
In prehistoric days, if you're a part of the herd, doesn't matter if you're a gazelle or deer or human
beings.
If you're away from the herd, you're vulnerable.
Some lion or tiger bear can see just you zoom in on you, grab you, kill you and eat you.
So when you're standing up to speak the whole herd, you were with the audience.
They're over there.
You're now standing.
You're the only person everyone can see.
So from an evolutionary, biological standpoint, it makes sense to be nervous.
So your body is sending adrenaline throughout everywhere in your veins.
And because of that, your brain is shutting down because your body is saying, don't think run.
And that's why if you've ever noticed, your palms might get wet.
If you weren't wearing shoes, you would notice the bottoms of your feet are getting wet.
That's because your body is preparing you for flight.
Your body is preparing to run away from what it senses is a dangerous situation.
You being isolated from the crowd now.
The good news is, even though on some college campuses, the audience can be rude or heckle.

you and eat you.
That's just not likely to happen.

--- Potential Disasters ---

There are a lot of different kinds of teleprompter's these days, some of them you can adjust with an
old fashioned knob yourself, some of them with a mouse, some of them with a foot pedal, and others
you have an actual teleprompter operator, someone else doing it for you.
There are pitfalls with all of these, and there are certain things you need to do to protect yourself.
And I want to go over some of those steps right now so that you're not left unguarded.
If you are going to have another teleprompter operator moving it, you've got to rehearse with that
person and you have to make sure that person is following you.
Otherwise, you get back to the same speech, the same tone.
The reason that people do this is they are afraid that the words are going to go off the screen and
they won't know what to say.
So you have to be in sync with your teleprompter operator.
If you pause, they better stop, because if they keep rolling and you're pausing, you're up a creek
without a paddle, you are in big, big trouble.
So you need to find somebody who's reliable, someone willing to practice with you, or you got to think
twice about even using a teleprompter.
The next thing you have to be prepared for is a teleprompter is used as a part of a computer, even
if it's an iPhone.
Guess what about computers?
They break, they have glitches, they malfunction.
They like electricity, they get bugs in them.
All of which to say is you still need to have your speech on paper, at least notes.
I prefer having notes consolidated on a single sheet.
But if you really want to get every single word just right, you better have it all on paper, because
paper doesn't require electricity.
Paper doesn't have glitches on it typically.
So it's a good fallback.
I hope you don't have to use it, but it's there if you need it.
There's all sorts of problems that can happen with computers.
Most famously, when Bill Clinton was president and giving his nineteen ninety five State of the Union,
what happened was it was uploaded into the teleprompter software as State of the Union.
When the person uploaded it, it said, Do you want to delete State of the Union now?
What do I want to do that I'm putting in it?
So person put no.
And there it was.
State of the Union is in the teleprompter.
He thought everything was fine.
President Clinton gets up to give his State of the Union.
He looks at it and he instantly realizes, oh, no, that's last year's State of the Union.
So he turns around.
The whole world is watching whispers to Vice President Gore and says, call Stephanopoulos and get the
correct speech.
We have last year's speech.
Now, Bill Clinton even then was an extraordinarily.
Experienced public speaker, a gifted public speaker, and has, according to many, a near photographic
memory, so he was able to give the first 10 minutes of his speech in a way that no one had any idea
there was a problem.
But you don't want to have to rely on that.
So assume nothing.
Practice.
Make sure you've got a safety habit on paper and do that and you will minimize your chances of disaster.

got exactly seven minutes and twenty eight seconds for your slot on prime time, that may be a good
reason, but many people use a teleprompter because they think it gives them greater control.
Not really, because if you do a bad job on the teleprompter, you're not controlling the outcome.
The outcome of any speech is not what comes out of your mouth.
It's what do people remember, what do they retain so they can act upon it.
So if you're reading a teleprompter in a wooden, stiff, phony way, the only outcome is people have
a negative impression of you and don't remember anything you said.
So that's an illusion to think that that's somehow safer, it's not safer, and it's not saving you
time.
Many people use the teleprompter because they think it will save the prep time, as we talked about
in the previous lecture.
It doesn't save time for most people.
Most of the time, they're far better off using a simple page of notes to speak for most business executives
and for that matter, most politicians.
The real danger of a speech is not that they got one word wrong, one comma wrong.
And suddenly there's tremendous criticism that does happen for presidents of countries or heads of of
federal banking systems that can happen.
But for most people, most of the time, the biggest problem in our speech is not that we got one word
wrong and there's a lot of criticism.
The biggest danger for most of us is we're so boring, nobody remembers anything we said.
So that's why I would urge you focus your time on making your speeches interesting and memorable.
And I've got other courses to deal with that.
That's not the point of this course, but that should be your focus, having an interesting speech and
delivering it in the best possible way.
Don't use a teleprompter because everyone else is don't use a teleprompter because there is some technician
who's sort of running the conference and says, well, everyone else is you have to be there.
The only reason to use a teleprompter is you've decided that will help you communicate most effectively
with your audience.
That's the only reason to use a teleprompter.
So, for example, I've been speaking to you for this entire course, and I'm not using a teleprompter
there plenty of times when I do use teleprompters.
But I didn't need one for this course because this is all material I've given hundreds of times to my
clients in real life.
So I know this.
So I didn't use a teleprompter.
So please give real thought to what is the best way for you to communicate with your audience.
And it may in fact be notes and not using a teleprompter, but make the judgment based on what will
help the audience, not what might save you time.

--- Secrets from Reagan ---

You heard me mention at the beginning the reason to use a teleprompter is not to save time, but to
really make sure everything goes right and you get the exact wording and phrasing the way you want it.
Now, people think of Ronald Reagan is one of the great communicators of all time.
He was called the great communicator.
Regardless of your politics, most fair minded people would say Ronald Reagan was a great speaker.
Now, many assume that was because he was an actor and had a lot of experience in front of cameras.
That's partially it.
But the real reason is he brought an actor's discipline of rehearsal to the public speaking process.
So when Reagan had a major speech like the State of the Union address, he would practice the speech
out loud for three hours a night, for a week.
Now, he wasn't doing that to memorize the speech.
He was using a teleprompter.
He was doing that to build a comfort with the words relationship with the words, to get his brain and
mouth and everything in sync used to having those words come out of his mouth in a set way.
After all that practice out loud, he would still spend an entire day practicing on video with the teleprompter,
again, not doing it to memorize, but doing it so he could get the pauses just right.
The emphasis just right head movements just right, so if Ronald Reagan could spend a whole day doing
videotape rehearsal for his teleprompter speeches, what's your excuse for not spending at least an
hour doing it?
There's always time for anything that's important.
If there's no time to practice your speech or teleprompter speech on video, maybe you shouldn't make
time to give the speech at all.
So please, please practice on video.
That's the real secret of the master communicators.

--- Setting Speaking Fees ---

They're doing it to get in front of a larger audience to sell albums and CDs.

--- Tricks for Look Good on Camera - Presentation Skills ---

So let me address the number one reason most people don't present online where you actually see them.

They're afraid of looking stupid, scared, nervous, uncomfortable, unflattering, double chin show,

We all have some level of vanity.

The number one problem most people have when they are presenting online is the phrase, I'm here today

mouth.
So the best thing you can do is to move move the way you do when you're normally relaxed, talking to

Now, it's easier to say that than it is to do it.
You're going to have to practice.

Now you'll see my head is still moving.
You want to move your head, you want to move your face.
You also want to move your body.
And you do want to move your hands.
Now, even though you might not see my hands, my hands are moving because when you move your hands,
your body moves more, your voice has more fluctuation to it.
Those things will have you looking relaxed and comfortable.
So you want movement.
The next thing you have to remember, it's you've got to lean forward a little bit.
Now, I'm standing for this.
It's probably going to be easier for you to be sitting.
This is just how I have my studio setup.
But if you're doing this from your laptop or your desktop, no reason why you can't see it.

If you're sitting back relaxed, you're going to look like you have a double chin.

and nervous.
You need to lean forward about 15 degrees into the camera.
So here from a side view, you can now see I am leaning forward.

The other thing that's crucial, your eyes, if you're trying to look at the camera and then you have
your notes up on the wall or a teleprompter over here, you become literally shifty eyed.

down, looking at notes and coming back and doing it again.
But most of the time, you should be looking at the camera.
The key, of course, is you have to keep moving your head because if your head freezes and nothing
else is moving again, looks like a robot.
You don't seem believable.
The other thing that's important on camera shield, a little bit of a smile, because if if you're just
like this and talking like this, it's going to make your face look blank, scared, flat, uninterested.

--- Learn the Secret to Speaking to Large Audiences ---

I've got good news and I've got bad news, the good news is it's actually pretty easy to speak in front
of large crowds, a thousand five thousand one hundred thousand.
All you have to do is the same thing you do when you're talking to one friend or colleague and you're
relaxed and animated, interesting and being conversational and telling stories and examples.
That's the good news.
The bad news is me simply telling you that doesn't make it any easier because we as human beings are
hardwired to be nervous about speaking in front of large crowds.
What happens is we tense up, our heart starts racing, we get scared, our brain stops working, our
memory stops working in our bodies, telling us, run our hands, get sweaty.
Well, why is that?
It is important before we really go deep into this and get great at it, to understand a little bit
of the background.
Evolutionary biologists believe we as human beings are hardwired to fear public speaking because public
speaking is essentially being separated from the crowd, separated from the herd and prehistoric times.
If we are in the jungle and we're a part of the herd, there's safety in numbers.
If there's two thousand other water buffalo with us or any sort of animal and a lion or a tiger bear
comes, our odds are pretty good one.
We'll get it out of the herd.
But the other one thousand nine hundred, we'll be safe.
So there's safety in numbers.
The old cliche is true.
If we're completely separated from the herd, if we're just all alone in the open field and animals
and other other predators of ours can see us from every direction, we're vulnerable.
We could be eaten, attacked.
That's not good.
So that's why many scientists believe that we as human beings are so nervous about speaking, especially
in front of large crowds.
That's why our bodies react differently.
That's why our hands get wet, moisture coming out, moisture coming out of our feet, too, because
our bodies telling us, don't think, run.
Now, you may have noticed if you ever tried to turn the page of a book, if you go like that, there's
more friction.
It's easier to turn that page the same way if you all of a sudden have to run through a jungle for your
life, having moisture coming out of your hands in the palm of your feet gives you more traction.
You can grab vines, swing away, and it's better for protection.
Your body's telling you run.
You've got that adrenaline rush, more energy.
But that's also when your body isn't working well from the neck up, you don't have the ability to think
clearly necessarily or to recall information because your body's telling you to spend all of your energy
running.
And it makes perfect sense if you're in the jungle about to be attacked.
Unfortunately, if you're about to give a speech in front of a major trade show conference of two thousand
people, that particular response isn't very helpful.
All it does is get in your way.

--- Pause for Maximum Affect and Impact ---

Here's one thing that is little different about speaking in front of large audiences, the difference
is you need a little more of a pause between your big thoughts.
It takes a while for your sound to simply travel all the way around a large room, regardless of the

You help yourself by having a little more of a pause between your thoughts, a little more of a transition
and allows the sound to filter out through the room and allows people to process it.
Part of it is they can't see your lips and your mouth as well as if it were just a room of 20 people

words to flow through the room or through the audience.
So keep that in mind with the speech, especially given that you might be nervous.
And when we're nervous, we tend to speak faster than usual.

--- Your Message Can Move Millions ---

Motivational speaking is about talking to a crowd, it could be a crowd of two, could be a crowd of
two thousand two hundred thousand and inspiring them through your words, through your own personal
story of how to do great things, how you've done great things, how you've accomplished things in life,
and how they can accomplish things in life.
That's what you have to be if you want to be a motivational speaker.
It's not simply about presenting facts, presenting data, PowerPoint slides, making a rational argument.
You have to have substance, but you have to have emotion fused together in a way that really makes
people understand you but feel they have to connect with you, the head and the heart level.
That's what makes a great motivational speaker.
I'm going to walk you through step by step now.
The things you need to do to put together your own motivational speech and to get the skill set you
need in order to deliver it.

--- How to Make Sure You Have a Motivating Message ---

My first question for you is, are people genuinely motivated by you, people who know you, people
who work with you, family, friends?
Is there something about you that is inspiring?
Because it's very hard to just cook this up.
It's not simply a matter of writing something out, practicing performance skills.
There's got to be something there.
So the first thing I'm going to ask you to do is really examine your life, the things you've overcome.
What adversity have you made it through?
What about it that you've done is impressive to people.
Now, if you were born as one famous motivational speaker was to a one parent family labeled --
poor, and you went on to have success in politics and media.
Well, that's a very inspirational story.
How do you go from down here to way up here?
That's obviously inspirational.
And I'm talking about Les Brown.
On the other hand, what if you're born on Park Avenue?
A wealthy, wealthy parents want all the finest schools, the greatest education, and you ended up
rich.
That's not very motivational to most people because they can't relate to that.
And they think, well, you already started life on third base.
But Michael Eisner, the former CEO of Disney, is in fact a motivational speaker at conferences because

--- Conclusion to Investor Pitching ---

Should I read my speech to make sure I don't make any mistakes?
Well, if you ask any presentation coach, this is probably the question we get that drives us bonkers
the most, it's virtually impossible to read a speech without, by definition, making a mistake.
You've destroyed all eye contact with the audience.
You've become boring, bland, most likely monotone.
Now, it is true there are some people good at reading speech.
Ronald Reagan was good at reading a speech.
I've seen Dan Rather read a speech.
Well, but guess what?
He was reading teleprompter copy and reading scripts every day for 60 years.
If you're reading scripts every day for 60 years, yeah, you'll probably get good at it.
But for most people, business people, people in public life, political life, it's really not a good
idea to read a speech because it instantly handcuffs you, destroys your eye contact, robs you of natural
rhythm in your voice.
Makes you sound phony, contrived, and it just evens out the towns, the volumes, the speed, the
pitch, it makes things to consistent and that's boring.
So you may think it's safe to read because that way you won't forget something.
But if you destroy people's ability to pay attention because they've fallen asleep, it's actually not
safe at all.
Reading a speech, in my view, is actually the riskiest thing you could ever do if your goal is to
actually communicate.

--- Culture is Everything ---

There's the classic image of the ugly American in a foreign country who's upset that everybody in this
country, whether it's Italy or whether it is Malaysia, doesn't speak English.
Now, it's inexcusable for Americans to be like that, but it is true.

to you loudly and slowly so you will understand my language.
Obviously, that doesn't work if the person you're speaking to doesn't speak your language.
Now, here's the part that's a little bit confusing or contradictory.

than normal and a little slower than normal now.
Hey, we all have cultural biases.
I have a bias.
I'm an American.
I only speak English.
But what I have found in speaking all over the world is there's a tremendous number of people who,
even if English is not their first language, they have a working understanding of English because they've
seen so many movies from Hollywood TV shows in English, they have learned a lot of English.
So here's where speaking a little bit slower helps.
It's simply easier for people to process what you're saying.
When it's slower, they can see the separation between words.
It's easy to sort of hear it figure out in their mind what is that word that they remembered studying
in English class five years ago.
And then they have to translate it from the English word to the word in their language.
That takes time.
Now, I'm not suggesting that you speak like this in a robotic way, because that's annoying.
That's really not suggesting that.
But what I am suggesting is speak a little bit slower than normal.
Don't be afraid to pause a little more between sentences, thoughts, paragraphs, feel free to walk
a little more, pause, reflect, look at people's eyes to see that there is some connection going on.
So it's a subtle thing, but I do recommend speaking a little bit slower than normal.
Longer pauses.
It's going to be much easier for the people in the audience who are translating in their own brain.
But it's also going to make life much easier for the translator because professional translators are
doing an awful lot.
But it's still tough to be speaking out to the audience at the same time having to listen to you.
So when you pause occasionally, they can then say what you just did in the other language, and yet
they haven't missed anything from what you're saying.
So that's the beauty of pausing.
And also just speaking a little louder than normal is going to make it easier for anyone to comprehend
it.
Again, you're not yelling.
You're not shouting.
You're not the so-called ugly American.
But a little louder, more pausing will make it much, much easier for everyone to understand and translate
in their own brains.
And that's going to make it more effective for your speech in your presentation.

The other thing that happens is they freeze their body, they freeze their face, and it's just a complete
disaster.
So if you want to be great at the teleprompter, there are a few simple rules you have to follow.
Number one, you have to sometimes speak a little louder than usual sometimes.
Number two, you have to speak a little softer than usual sometimes.
Number three, you have to speak a little faster than usual.
Number four, sometimes you have to speak a little slower than usual.
And number five, sometimes you have to pause.
It really comes down to that if you do all of those things, plus have some natural head and hand and
facial expression, if you do that, you won't sound like you're reading a teleprompter.
Now, there are certain politicians well known for doing a good job with a teleprompter, not being
partisan here.
Ronald Reagan and Barack Obama both great with a teleprompter.
Now they have different messages, different philosophies.
But the way they used a teleprompter was exactly the same.
They changed their speed tempo volume.
They paused and they sounded as if they were just talking to you.
The other thing they do is they rehearse.
People use the teleprompter because they think, great, I won't have to rehearse or memorize.
Now, I can just talk.
Now, if you want to use the teleprompter effectively, it actually requires more time.
You need to practice that speech.
You need to get used to it.
Here's the final thing I want to say about teleprompter is don't let someone talk you into using it
if you really don't need it.
A lot of major national conventions, trade conventions are somehow convincing their executives to do
this because it gets things on time.
No, it doesn't.
It tends to make everyone really boring and flat.
Most people most of the time are much better off speaking from a simple sheet, one sheet of paper rather
than having the whole script.
Now, something else you can do with your teleprompter is you can use it just to put notes or an outline.
So if you're going to use teleprompter, by all means, practice, rehearse, rehearse on video, it's
not something to do to save you time.
It's something you use if you have even more time than usual to practice and rehearse.

--- Using Alcohol to Calm Your Nerves before a Speech Public Speaking ---

OK, you have to give that big presentation after dinner, is it OK for you to take that glass of wine
or that shot of Snopes to calm you down before your presentation?
Folks, I'm not trying to turn you into a teetotaller or remove fun from your life, but here's the
problem with having even a glass or two of wine or beer before you're giving a speech, you may think
it's calming you down.
It may make you feel calm for the moment.
But here's the problem.
Alcohol can slow your brain down even a little bit.
If you're nervous, you're already having a harder time recalling information, pulling out what you
planned on, saying if you have alcohol in you, it can slow you down another half second.
But that can seem like five seconds when you're standing up in front of people that can actually make
you more nervous.
This inability to pull out certain facts or numbers that you wanted to hit in your presentation.
So I would not recommend drinking any alcohol before you give a speech.
The other problem is for some people that can make them read other people, it could make them overheated,
even a glass or two.
And that little bit of shine perspiration can make you look like you're more nervous than you are.
Finally, if you are the main speaker after dinner, people are coming up to you afterwards.

Fine, but you're sort of a celebrity at that moment.

--- Taking Beta-Blockers to Calm Your Nerves Public Speaking ---

Should you take beta blockers to calm your nerves before giving a big speech or presentation?

They can help with nerves.

If you're nervous about how you're presenting, it may be with good reason.
It may be that you're Boehringer.
You haven't really thought of good ideas and good examples and good stories.
The way to get over that is not to mask the feeling with a drug, but it's to actually make sure you
have a good speech, a good presentation.
So you should start by rehearsing on video.

to feel better and feel like I'm good looking, or is the answer to actually take a shower, shave,
look in the mirror and be able to see, OK, I'm now presentable.
So that's my problem with the whole beta blocker thing.
It's it's not dealing with the real problem.

The real problem is do you actually have an interesting, compelling, memorable presentation?

So take my advice.
Do not spend time tracking down doctor's going to pharmacies, getting beta blockers.

--- If my allotted time is cut, what should I eliminate Public Speaking ---

What do you do if you have been told you have to give a 30 minute presentation, you're about to stand
up and the organizer says, hey, we're running late instead of 30 minutes, speak for just 15 minutes.
Classic dilemma when your time is cut short.
Here's what most people do, they speak twice as fast and they throw away all their interesting examples,
case studies and stories, and they waste a lot of time saying, I know I can speak really quick because
I don't have a lot of time.
They tell me to make this fast.
So I'm not going to be able to cover all my.
And they waste time talking about their time.
Huge mistake.
Never talk about the time you have or the lack of time or how you thought you had more time.
Simply use the time you have for maximum effect.
Use every second to put a spotlight on an idea that's important to you, that's also important to your
audience.
And if you had 30 minutes of material planned and now you have 15, you need to chop in half the number
of key points you were trying to convey, because it does absolutely no good whatsoever to strip away
the examples, case studies and stories for your points just to cover more points, because no one's
going to remember the points yet.
They're that important.
Give them the PDF, give them handouts, give them a whole book if you want.
But don't try to speak quickly at an abstract level, doing a data dump, use your normal tone of voice,
your normal speed, just do fewer points and flesh out each one with stories and case studies.
And this way they may even ask you to spend more time talking.
If not, people will go out of their way to try to get your PDF, your PowerPoint presentation, or
go to your website to find out more information.
You can give a great presentation regardless of the time limitations given you, even if it's a last
minute change.

--- The One Big Secret to Beating an Incumbent ---

Are you running against an incumbent?
If so, that is a different type of a race.
It's a unique race.
It's not like an open race and it simply may the best man, may the best woman run.
And things are in a hat if you're running against an incumbent.
Keep in mind, unless the incumbent is in jail or halfway to jail, that incumbent has a huge, huge
advantage, an advantage in name recognition, staff, time, money, endorsements, campaign organization
doesn't mean you can't win, but you do have to make the case as to why that incumbent deserves to be
fired.
Now, you don't have to necessarily use that language, but that's what you're asking voters to do if
you're running to replace a sitting city councilman Councilwoman.
You've got to make the case to the constituents in your district that this person needs to be fired.
They need to be replaced.
So what you're really doing is telling the voters they made a mistake.
Again, you're not going to couch it in those terms, but that's essentially the argument you're making.
And most voters don't like to admit to making mistakes.
Most people don't like to admit to making mistakes.
Think of it this way.
If you are desperate for an administrative assistant and I come to you and I say, look, I've got great
credentials, resume references, here they are.
I type two hundred words a minute and you really need someone.
I may have a good chance of being hired by you, but if you have an administrative assistant and this
person has worked for you for 10 years and you know this person as a single parent who supports two
children and has not the most competent person in the world, but basically gets along well with everyone
in the office, is an honest person and maybe types 40 words a minute.
Are you going to fire that person to bring me on?
Even though I type two hundred words a minute?
Chances are, no, it's human nature not to want to fire people who are already there.
So, so much of your challenge, if you're running against an incumbent, is you've got to make the
case as to why this person should be fired.
What have they done that was incompetent?
What votes do they cast that were really detrimental to the citizens?
What initiatives did they fail to support that were needed by this political jurisdiction?
You've got to make the case.
Now, I'm not suggesting you throw mud or you go through their bed sheets or through their trash.
What I am suggesting is you have to look at the public record.
What have they done, what have they not done?
And this should, in fact, relate to why you're running, because presumably if the incumbent is doing
everything well, there's no rational reason for you to run other than vanity or ego.
You don't want people to think that.
And I hope that's not the case.
So if you're running against an incumbent, you've got to give one main reason, something they've done
that's either incompetent, ineffective, perhaps corrupt or unethical.
But you've got to really tell people why this person does not deserve their trust anymore, why this
person does not deserve their vote an additional time and why you can do better.
That is your challenge when you're running against an incumbent.
If you say, well, T.J., I don't want to be negative, I just want to say my own platform, my own
credentials, and let the voters decide again, unless that incumbent is halfway to jail or cited for
major ethical violations, you're not going to win just by saying what's good about you.
You're going to have to make the case as to why the other person should be fired.
Back to my example earlier about your administrative assistant.
As I laid it out before, you're not going to fire that administrative assistant.
But if I can give you evidence showing your administrative assistant has embezzled a hundred thousand
dollars from you and that the authorities are about to arrest this person, well, now, maybe you might
actually hire me as your assistant.
Now, you might not want me for a variety of reasons, but I think you get my point.
You're going to have to make the case in a factual, substantive manner as to why the incumbent should
be fired and you should replace that incumbent.

--- Speaking to The Media ---

If you're running for public office, you had better get used to talking to the news media.

And I would say no, losing candidates accomplish that.

--- Always Select Your Best Persuasion Opportunities and Environments ---

There is a clear cut hierarchy for which way of communicating with someone is more persuasive.
Now, I can't speak for every single industry, but in general, I want to give you some principles
that do apply face to face meeting.
Talking to one person is in general the most persuasive way of talking someone into something.
Think of it.
Those of you who are married, did you either propose to someone or accept a proposal through an email,
a voice mail, a certified letter, a video?
Probably not.
It was a face to face meeting.
So if you want to increase your ability to be more persuasive, part of what you've got to do is look
at all the other things you do to interact with clients, colleagues, customers, prospects, bosses,
and try to figure out how can you get to more face to face meetings, either one on one or presentations

--- Moving the Numbers Game In Your Favor ---

This next insight will sound like a cliche to you, it is, but I want to dig a little deeper and bring

--- Never Bore With Data Dumps Again ---

I'm a big believer in teaching people in the positive and not just a bunch of don't, don't, don't,
don't do this a series of negatives, but I do want to address the elephant in the room.
In my experience, the number one factor of people not being persuasive is they all make the same mistake.
The mistake is they have an opportunity to pitch, to present, to try to persuade someone in their
organization, in the workplace or a client outside.
And they waste the opportunity by just doing a massive data dump.
They tell the person in the organization or the prospect, every single fact they know, they try to
educate the person on every part of the process, every fact, the history.
And they think, oh, I'm being thorough, I'm being hard working.
The person is going to be so impressed that I'm so knowledgeable.
And I covered everything.
I didn't leave anything out.
No one can accuse me of being superficial and leaving anything out.
It's a very defensive negative mentality.
And the result is typically the person you're trying to persuade isn't persuaded because they're just
lost in this sea of data.
So do not make that mistake.
We're going to spend some time in the next few lectures helping you figure how do you narrow it down?
How do you really refine what's truly most important?
As Mark Twain once said and a lot of other successful writers have claimed to say this, I'm sorry I
wrote you a long letter, I didn't have time to write you a short letter.
It actually takes more time, thought intelligence to narrow your messages down than to just say absolutely
everything.
So we've all been guilty of this.

--- Master the Process Of NOT Telling People Too Much About Your Process ---

What else makes people profoundly non persuasive?
It's not just the data dump, it's the specific things they're putting into that data dump.
One big challenge, one big problem for so many people is they want to explain every single part of
the process of what they're going to do to help someone and therefore why that person should then use
them or put a rubber stamp of approval on what they're asking for.
In general, human beings don't care about the process unless it's their full time job.
They care about the results you will give them.
This is true whether it's a client, a prospect, a boss or a colleague in another department, focus
on the benefits to the person you're trying to persuade.
That means you cannot go into every single little detail on the process.
It means you cannot describe every little feature.
Now, unfortunately, a lot of us, when we are so excited about what we do, our profession, we want
to tell everybody everything we do and we think this is good and people like our passion for it.
But if we're overwhelming them with the process, we can, in fact, work against ourselves.
We can be less persuasive.
Now, this can happen to anyone.
A few years ago, this even happened to me, I found myself when I was giving a sales presentation,
a pitch trying to persuade someone to hire me for a day of public speaking, training or media training.
I went on and on and on into the process, and I would send them a nice personalized video, but I would
then walk them through every step of the process.
I would tell them what we'll have our pre training conference call and you'll hear you'll send me a
video and I'll critique it in advance.
And then during the day of presentation training, I'll get you on camera a dozen times.
And after that, you'll have Skype follow up with me and you can text or email or call me with questions
and I'll answer you in a video back and you can go back into the online training school at any point.
And I'll send you follow up training videos every single day for the next year.
I went on and on and on.
And truth is, some of the people who hired me did like that level of detail, but.
A lot or other people, other prospects were just overwhelmed.
I spent too much time talking about the process of every little thing I'm going to do to help them become
a better presenter.
And what I should have done is focused on the benefits to them.
So now when someone pitches me or ask me for a pitch, I focus on the benefits.
I say, hey, if you work with me, I'm going to make sure you are more comfortable, confident, relaxed,
any time you speak.
Doesn't matter if it's in front of one person, one hundred, a thousand or ten thousand people.
I'm going to really give you the skills so that you'll know in advance your audience will understand
you.
And here's the tricky part.
I'm going to make sure your audience will actually remember your key messages, because most speakers
are so boring, no one remembers anything.
And because of that, there's a much greater chance that you will persuade your audience to do what
you want.
And in this case, I personalize it and and fill in the blanks of what I know that person's trying to
accomplish.
Sal, do whatever it is.
So that pitch only takes me 60 seconds or so in a video.

So you have to catch yourself on this and make sure you don't accidentally fall into the temptation
of more.
Is more is more narrow the focus.
This is especially true if it's one sided communication.
You're sending someone a video, an email, you're talking to them over the phone or in a Skype video.
But there's other people there and it's not quite a one on one conversation.
It's a little bit different when it's a one on one meeting.

If they have questions about all the other process, by all means, answer their questions in detail.
But when you have the open floor to just start off, focus on your benefits, don't tell people every
part of your process.

--- The Proper Job Interview Mindset ---

--- The Strategy Memo ---

I want to give you one very, very specific advanced tip that I believe will help distinguish you from
all the other people who get a job interview with this organization.
And here's the tip.
Don't simply walk in with an extra copy of your resume.
Of course, you do need a copy of the resume, even though they should have one on file, or how would
they have called you for the interview?
You do need another paper.
People still do like to read paper, sometimes paper copy of your resume.
But I would also suggest you have another sheet of paper.
It's a one page memo.
And in this one page memo, I would spend twenty five thirty percent of the page summarizing what you
think are the key strategic strengths of this organization.
What this is doing is it's showing you've done your research that you can write, that you can communicate,
that you can process information and that you value the organization, that you see what they're doing
well.
But the bottom two thirds of the page, I would come up with suggestions, ideas, whatever you want
to call it, on how to improve the organization.
Now, there is some risk to this because someone could always be offended.
Well, they are criticizing something I'm doing by suggesting we need to do this.
But here's what I've noticed.
Most employers are impressed by anyone who's given time and thought and energy to how to improve things.
So coming up, with just 10 ideas, it could be bullet points of very specific things the organization
can do, perhaps a little differently.
A new market to enter, perhaps an ebook on a particular topic to reach certain customers, come up
with 10 ideas and present that in the interview, say, hey, I'm so excited about this company.
What I've learned about you, I hope you don't mind, but I took it upon myself to do a brief memo on
what I think the key strategic assets are of your company and possible areas for improvement.
I realize I certainly don't know everything at this point, but I do want you to have a sense of my
general thought process.
I'm willing to bet that ninety eight percent of the time, if you did that, an employer would be extraordinarily
impressed because even bad ideas are better than no ideas.
What you're doing in this memo is you're talking about them, not yourself.
Here's the little secret about job interviews.
The more you talk about that person, that company, that organization, the less about yourself, the
better off you are.
People care about themselves.
They care about their organization.
They care about how you are going to help them.
They're not hiring you just to help the unemployment rate.
They're hiring you because you can somehow make their life easier, help them make more money, help
them serve more customers, clients, patients.
Everything you do has to be focused on that.
And that's why this little secret strategy, a one page memo, I'm not suggesting quit your other part
time jobs, stop job hunting and write some 30 page treatise, just a one page memo, spend an hour
on it and come up, brainstorm ideas on how this organization can be better.
Even if you just have one good idea and the others are horrible, they're likely to remember that idea.
Even if they think all of your ideas are horrible, they're going to be impressed that you took the
initiative to create something, to produce something.
And they can see that you can write clearly, that you can write concisely, and that you can present
a proposal that's going to go a long way towards distinguishing you in this job interview.
I can tell you I've never had anyone do that in a job interview with me, but if they did, pretty good
chance I would hire them.

--- Ask for the Job ---

So you've accomplished everything you want of the job interview, you feel like it went well, how do

You don't want to just look at your watch.
Oh, I know you've got other people to interview.
Let me get out of here.

You need some way of concluding.
That's graceful and that's positive.
That ends with the ask.
What I mean by that is in a sincere way, a non pushy way.
Ask for the job, not be sincere about this.
Sometimes you get into a job interview and you can tell you would hate this job.
It's not a good fit.
They wouldn't like you.
You wouldn't like them, in which case you just thank people for their time.
But let's say you're in a job interview.
It goes well.
It seems like a great company or a great organization.
You'd like to work there.
You legitimately think you're a good fit and you have the skills.
Don't just thank the person and say thanks for your time.
Instead, sum up.
Say, you know, I really appreciate you taking the time to tell me more about your company now that
I know X, Y and Z and mentioned something specific, I think that really is a perfect fit for me based
on X, Y and Z.
Something else in your background, tie in together, your strengths, your passions.
Bring in something new that came out from this job interview.
Show the person you're really listening to them, but make the case how this is a good fit.
And then the final thing is and you got to be sincere about this show moment of reflection.
You know, now that I think about this, I really think this would be a good fit.
I would like to have this job, and I sincerely hope you consider me for this job.
Ask again, you don't want to seem pushy.
You certainly don't want to seem desperate.
So please give me this job or I'm going to get kicked out of my apartment.
Now, you never want to seem like you need a job, but there's nothing wrong with seeming like you'd
really like this job.
You're not stating I have 50 other job offers.
You're not implying it directly, but there has to be not a single whiff of desperation or intense need.
Instead, it has to be.
You've thought about it.
You like what you hear today.
You're implying this has been a mutual interview.
I'm interviewing you to see if your company is good enough for me.
I've thought about it and I've concluded this is a good fit.
So not only thank you for your time, but thank you for your consideration.
I would in fact like this job, ask for the job.
We've all heard the story of a politician who spent a lot of time with the voter and the voter said
he liked the politician, she liked the politician, but didn't vote for him.
And you say what?
He didn't ask for my vote.
A lot of times in life you don't get if you don't ask.
So my recommendation is ask in a non threatening, non pushy non need to ask for the job, do that.
And then there's no doubt whatsoever in the mind of the interview that if everything else fits, you
would be a good selection for this job.
Good luck with your job interviews and good luck with your career.

--- How to Deliver a Eulogy Public Speaking ---

--- Giving the Presentation So That It's Not About You ---

A ceremonial speech is by definition a formal speech, though I get a little nervous when people use
the phrase formal speech in most situations, because typically what the average speaker means is I'm
giving a formal presentation is they want to have a license to do a boring data dump to tell people,
their board of directors about everything they've done in the last quarter.
It may feel formal because you're in a stuffy boardroom and people are important that you're talking
to.
But if you make it formal in the sense of I'm going to be stiff and straight and read, especially if
it's for 10, 15, 20 minutes, that's not a formal speech.
That's an awful speech.
That's a boring speech because you're not saying anything that's particularly interesting and memorable,
which is the goal of most presentations.
Ceremonial presentations are different.
You're not trying to come up with new concepts.
You're not trying to dazzle people with your cleverness, with your original ideas.
In fact, this is a time to take the spotlight off of you and put the spotlight back on the office or
the occasion, whether it's the wedding, whether it is the funeral, it's a way of getting people to
reflect on larger values, eternal values, things that are not new and things that are not associated
with your ideas.
You're there to simply put a spotlight on that and to help the process of a particular activity.
So that's what's very different about ceremonial speeches.
In some ways, it does make it easier.
You don't have to go out of your way to juice it up to make it more invigorating or exciting.
You're not trying to put your personal stamp on the ceremonial speech as much.
So please keep that in mind.
This is the one time when you're giving a presentation where your personality shouldn't overwhelm your
message.

--- Look Classy by NOT Talking About Honor or Nerves ---

it's not all about me, me, me, me, me.
So at the beginning of your ceremonial speech, I wouldn't talk about, oh, gosh, this is such a big
honor.
Wow.
I'm so honored.
There may be a point later on when you do have free reign to speak about the event and what's going
on.
But for the official ceremonial part, don't talk about what an honor it is for you.
Also, don't talk about how nervous you are.
Oh, my gosh, I'm nervous.
I hope I don't mess up the oath of office because it's not about you.
It's about what is actually going on.
The institutions involved don't make everything about you.
Don't talk about how you're feeling about this ceremonial speech, this ceremonial presentation.
Just deliver the presentation.

--- Understanding the Power of Note-Free Speaking ---

In today's lesson, we delve into the transformative power of effective communication, specifically
focusing on the art of speaking without relying on notes.
Imagine standing in front of an audience, your mind clear, your message powerful, and your delivery
flawless, all without the crutch of notes or prompts.
This is the pinnacle of public speaking, a skill that distinguishes good speakers from great ones.
To achieve this, we must first understand the psychological impact of note free speaking on both the
speaker and the audience.
When a speaker engages with their audience without the barrier of notes, it creates a connection that
is both authentic and compelling.
This connection is not just about eye contact, it's about the energy and confidence that flows from
the speaker to the audience, transforming the presentation into an impactful experience.
The journey to mastering note free speaking begins with the development of a strong memory.
Techniques such as the memory palace or the method of loci have been used for centuries by orators to
memorize speeches by associating pieces of information with specific locations in a mental image of
a physical space.
Speakers can recall details with ease.
This method not only improves memory, but also enhances the speaker's ability to visualize their speech,
creating a more dynamic and engaging delivery.
Another crucial aspect of note free speaking is the structure of the presentation.
A well-structured speech with a clear beginning, middle, and end aids in memorization and delivery.
It's about crafting a narrative that is not only easy for the speaker to remember, but also for the
audience to follow.
The use of storytelling techniques can be particularly effective as stories are more memorable than
abstract information.
By weaving key messages into a narrative, speakers can ensure that their points are not only heard
but remembered.
Practice, of course, is indispensable.
It is through repeated practice that the speaker becomes familiar with the material, not just on a
cognitive level, but on an emotional and physical one as well.
This familiarity breeds confidence, allowing the speaker to move beyond the words to deliver a message
with passion and conviction.
It's not about memorizing word for word, but internalizing the essence of the message so that it can
be communicated in a way that feels natural and spontaneous.
Lastly, embracing imperfection is a vital part of speaking without notes.
The fear of forgetting or making a mistake often holds speakers back from attempting note free presentations.
However, minor imperfections or deviations from the script can actually enhance a speaker's authenticity,
making them more relatable to the audience.
It's about being present in the moment, connecting with the audience, and communicating from the heart.
In conclusion, the ability to speak without notes is not just a skill, but an art form that elevates
the speaker audience connection to new heights.
It requires practice, confidence, and a deep understanding of one's material, but the rewards are
immeasurable.
By mastering this art, speakers can transform their presentations into memorable, impactful experiences
that resonate with their audience long after the speech has ended.

--- Shifting from Reading to Engaging ---

Transitioning from a script dependent speaker to a dynamic, engaging communicator is a transformative
journey.
It begins with understanding the power of connection over perfection.
The fear of forgetting lines or making mistakes often leads speakers to cling to their notes.
However, the essence of impactful speaking lies in the ability to connect with your audience on a personal
level, something that reading from a script can hinder.
To embark on this journey, start with the practice of distilling your message into key themes rather
than memorizing every word.
This approach shifts the focus from reciting to understanding and conveying the core message.
Think of your presentation as a story with a clear beginning, middle, and end.
Each section should flow naturally into the next, guided by the main points rather than scripted lines.
Visualization techniques can significantly aid this process, visualizing your speech as a series of
interconnected images or a pathway through a landscape can help embed your key points in memory.
This method, known as the Memory Palace technique, leverages spatial memory to recall information
in a vivid and structured way.
Another critical aspect is rehearsal.
However, the goal of rehearsal is not memorization but familiarity.
Rehearse your presentation in various settings and at different times of the day.
This variability helps build confidence in your ability to deliver your message under any circumstances.
Additionally, recording your rehearsals and watching them back can provide insights into areas for
improvement and increase your comfort with the material.
Engaging with your audience is also crucial.
Eye contact, for instance, can transform a presentation.
It makes your audience feel acknowledged and involved in the conversation.
Practice making eye contact with different parts of the audience throughout your presentation.
This practice helps in breaking the barrier between the speaker and the audience, making the experience
more interactive and personal.
Lastly, embracing imperfections is vital.
Authenticity resonates more with audiences than flawless delivery.
If you stumble over words, acknowledge it with grace and move on.
Your audience will appreciate your humanity and feel more connected to you as a speaker.
In conclusion, the transition from reading notes to engaging your audience is a journey of building
confidence in your message and yourself.
It involves understanding your material deeply, employing memory techniques, practicing extensively,
connecting with your audience, and embracing imperfections.
This approach not only enhances the delivery of your presentation, but also transforms the experience
for both you and your audience, making it more memorable and impactful.

--- The Basics of Memory and Recall in Public Speaking ---

Understanding the psychology behind memory and recall can significantly enhance your public speaking
skills.
Imagine delivering a powerful presentation, engaging your audience without once glancing at your notes.
This isn't a skill reserved for the few.
It's an art that can be learned and mastered with the right techniques.
Today we delve into the cognitive mechanisms that enable this feat and how you can apply them to your
presentations.
Memory is our brain's capability to encode, store, and retrieve information when needed.
It's a complex process involving different types of memory short term, long term, and working memory.
For public speaking, we focus primarily on long term memory and techniques to transfer information
from short term to long term memory efficiently.
One such technique is the method of loci, an ancient mnemonic strategy that involves visualizing a
familiar place and associating elements of your speech with specific locations within this mental landscape.
This method not only aids in memorization, but also makes recall smoother and more natural during your
presentation.
Another critical aspect is the role of understanding and personal connection in memory retention.
Information is more easily remembered when it has personal significance or when it's understood deeply
rather than superficially memorized.
This is why truly grasping your topic and connecting with it on a personal level can make a significant
difference in how well you remember your speech.
Integrating stories, anecdotes, or examples that resonate with you can also make the memorization
process more effective and the delivery more authentic.
Practice is, of course, indispensable.
Repeatedly rehearsing your speech out loud and in various settings helps solidify the information in
your long term memory.
Each rehearsal should aim to mimic the conditions of the actual presentation as closely as possible,
engaging not just your voice, but your body language and visual aids, if applicable.
This holistic approach to practice ensures that your delivery becomes second nature, allowing you to
focus on connecting with your audience rather than recalling your next line.
In conclusion, mastering the art of delivering presentations without notes is not just about memorizing
words.
It's about understanding your material.
Making a personal connection with it and practicing in a way that engages your whole being.
By employing memory enhancing techniques like the method of loci, making your material personally significant
and thorough practice, you'll be well on your way to captivating your audience with ease and confidence,
all without a glance at your notes.

--- Building a Structured Approach to Internalizing Content ---

Effective communication is the cornerstone of impactful presentations.
Yet the art of speaking without relying on notes is a skill that eludes many.
Today, we delve into strategies that enable you to deliver presentations with confidence, clarity
and conviction without the crutch of notes.
Imagine stepping onto the stage.
Your mind clear, your message internalized, and your audience captivated.
This is the power of mastering.
Note free presentations.
To begin, the foundation of any memorable presentation lies in its structure.
A well-structured presentation follows a logical flow, making it easier to internalize and recall.
Start with crafting a compelling opening that hooks your audience from the first word.
This could be a startling statistic, a poignant question, or a relatable anecdote.
The opening sets the tone and primes your audience for the journey they're about to embark on with you.
Following the opening, outline your key points in a logical sequence.
Each point should build upon the previous one, leading your audience through your presentation like
a story.
This narrative approach not only makes your presentation more engaging, but also simplifies the memorization
process.
Stories are inherently easier to remember than disjointed facts, because they connect with our emotions
and experiences.
To enhance your ability to recall these points.
Employ mental mapping techniques.
Mental mapping involves associating each key point with a specific image or concept, creating a mental
map of your presentation.
This technique taps into the visual and spatial memory systems, which are more robust than verbal memory
alone.
For instance, if your first key point is about innovation, you might visualize a light bulb.
When you reach this segment of your presentation, the image of the light bulb triggers your memory
of the associated content.
Another critical aspect is the practice of distillation.
Distill your content to its essence, focusing on the core message you want to convey.
This doesn't mean omitting necessary details, but rather ensuring every word serves a purpose.
The more concise your presentation, the easier it is to internalize and deliver without notes.
Repetition plays a crucial role in moving information from short term to long term memory.
Rehearse your presentation multiple times, focusing on the flow and the transitions between points.
With each repetition, your familiarity with the material increases, making it easier to recall during
the actual presentation.
Lastly, cultivate a mindset of flexibility.
Even with thorough preparation, be prepared to adapt your presentation in real time based on the audience's
reactions and feedback.
This adaptive approach not only makes your presentation more responsive, but also more engaging.
In summary, the ability to deliver presentations without notes is a skill that combines structure,
storytelling, mental mapping, distillation, repetition, and flexibility.
By mastering these techniques, you transform your presentations into memorable experiences for your
audience, establishing a deep connection and leaving a lasting impression.
Embrace these strategies and watch as your confidence and impact as a speaker soar to new heights.

--- Introduction to Mental Mapping for Presentations ---

Public speaking is an art that has evolved significantly over the years, transforming from a mere exchange
of information to a powerful tool for persuasion and leadership.
In today's fast paced world, the ability to deliver a compelling presentation without relying on notes
or is not just an asset, but a necessity for professionals across all sectors.
This lesson delves into the innovative technique of mental mapping, a strategy that enhances memory
recall and helps speakers deliver their message with confidence and clarity.

Each branch is further embellished with examples, stories, statistics, and other supporting details,
creating a rich, interconnected web of information.
One of the most compelling aspects of mental mapping is its versatility.
Whether you're delivering a technical presentation to experts in your field or a motivational speech
to a general audience, the technique can be tailored to suit any topic, audience, or objective.
Furthermore, mental mapping encourages the use of vivid imagery, metaphors, and personal anecdotes,
making your presentation not only memorable to the audience, but also easier for you to recall without
the need for notes.
Incorporating Mipmapping into your presentation.
Preparation requires practice and patience.
It begins with the creation of a physical map, which can be drawn on paper or created using digital
tools.
This initial step is crucial as it translates your thoughts into a visual format, making it easier
to memorize and internalize over time as you become more adept at creating and using mental maps.
You'll find that the need to refer to your physical map diminishes, allowing you to deliver your presentation
with greater freedom and dynamism.
In conclusion, mental mapping is a powerful technique that can transform the way you approach public

--- The Science Behind Effective Memory Techniques ---

Effective communication is at the heart of every successful presentation.
However, the ability to deliver these presentations without relying on notes is a skill that sets apart
good speakers from great ones.
Today, we dive into the science behind effective memory techniques that can empower you to speak confidently
and fluently without the crutch of notes.
Memory A complex cognitive process involves encoding, storing, and retrieving information.
Understanding this process is crucial for developing strategies to improve memory retention.
Techniques such as the method of loci, also known as the memory palace, leverage the brain's innate
spatial memory to recall information by associating pieces of information with specific locations in
a familiar place.
Speakers can effectively navigate through their presentation points as if walking through a physical
space.
Another powerful technique is the use of mnemonics.
These are tools that help us remember information through association using simple patterns of letters,
lists, or ideas.
For instance, acronyms where each letter stands for a word in a phrase can simplify complex information
into manageable, easily recallable chunks.
This method is particularly useful for remembering lists or sequences which are common in presentations.
Chunking is another strategy that breaks down information into smaller, more manageable units or chunks.
This approach is based on the concept that our short term memory can typically hold only a limited amount
of information at once.
By organizing information into chunks, we can improve our ability to remember and recall it during
a presentation.
Visualization is a technique that involves creating a mental image for the information that needs to
be remembered.
This.
This method is especially effective for visual learners who can recall images more easily than words.
By turning abstract data or concepts into vivid, concrete images, speakers can more readily access
this information during their presentations.
The Feynman Technique, named after the renowned physicist Richard Feynman, focuses on teaching the
content to someone else.
In simple terms, this method reinforces understanding and recall by forcing the speaker to simplify
and clarify their thoughts, making the information more memorable and easier to articulate without
notes.
Practice, of course, plays a critical role in memorizing presentations.
Rehearsing out loud repeatedly helps to solidify the memory of the presentations content.
It also aids in refining the delivery, making the speech more natural and engaging.
In conclusion, mastering the art of delivering presentations without reading from notes requires understanding
and applying effective memory techniques by leveraging methods like the Memory Palace, mnemonics,
chunking, visualization, and the Feynman Technique.
Speakers can enhance their memory retention and recall abilities coupled with diligent practice.
These strategies enable speakers to deliver powerful note free presentations, engaging their audience
with confidence and ease.
Embracing these techniques not only improves presentation skills, but also enriches overall communication
abilities, making them invaluable tools for any professional.

You make it accessible.

Making the technical details that follow easier to digest and understand.
In conclusion, storytelling is not just a way to entertain.

ultimately more memorable.

Tell a story.

--- Association Methods to Enhance Recall ---

Imagine stepping onto a stage, facing a sea of faces and delivering a powerful presentation without
once glancing at your notes.
Sounds daunting.
Not with the right techniques.
Today we'll dive into the art of association methods, a game changer for memorizing your speech and
connecting deeply with your audience.
Association methods hinge on the principle that our minds are better at recalling information linked
to vivid, sensory, rich images or stories.
This technique is not just about memorization.
It's about making your message memorable and engaging for your audience, ensuring it resonates long
after you've left the stage.
Let's start with the story method, a powerful tool in your arsenal.
This involves weaving key points of your presentation into a compelling narrative.
Humans are hardwired to remember stories much more effectively than isolated facts.
By embedding your message in a story, you create a mental journey for your audience, making complex
information accessible and memorable.
Next we explore the method of loci, an ancient technique dating back to Greek and Roman times.
This method involves visualizing a familiar place like your home, and placing mental images of the
key points of your presentation in different locations.
During your speech, you mentally walk through this space, triggering the recall of each point as you
see the associated image.
This not only aids in memorization, but also helps in structuring your presentation in a logical flow.
Mind mapping is another powerful technique, especially for visual learners.
It involves creating a diagram that represents connections between your presentations main idea and
its supporting points.
Each branch of the map is a visual cue, leading you through your content in a way that's easy to remember.
Mind maps are not only helpful in memorization phase, but also invaluable in the planning stages of
your presentation.
The Peg system is a method that works well for presentations with a list of items or key points.
It involves associating each point with a peg, usually a number or letter.
For instance, if you're presenting five key strategies, you might link each strategy to the fingers
on your hand during your presentation.
Recalling each finger will help you remember the associated strategy.
Lastly, the link method is a simple yet effective way to remember sequences of information.
This involves creating a story where each piece of information is linked to the next in a memorable
way.
The absurd or humorous the imagery, the more likely you are to remember it.
In conclusion, association methods are not just about improving your memory, they're about enhancing
the impact of your presentations.
By employing these techniques, you can deliver your message with confidence and flair, creating a
lasting impression on your audience.
Remember, the goal is not to memorize word for word, but to internalize your content so deeply that
you can speak from the heart, making genuine connections with your audience.

--- Mastering the Art of Impromptu Speaking ---

Effective communication is not just about what you say, but how you say it.
Today we'll dive into the art of persuasion in public speaking, a skill that can transform the impact
of your presentations and speeches.
Persuasion is the ability to influence your audience's beliefs, attitudes, intentions, motivations,
or behaviors through your words and delivery.
It's a powerful tool in the hands of a skilled speaker.
To begin, let's understand the three pillars of persuasion identified by Aristotle ethos, pathos,
and logos.
Ethos refers to the credibility or ethical appeal of the speaker.
This means establishing yourself as trustworthy and authoritative on your topic.
You can achieve this by sharing your experience, qualifications and demonstrating a clear, unbiased
understanding of your subject.
Pathos, on the other hand, appeals to the audience's emotions.
It's about connecting with them on a personal level, using stories, anecdotes and expressive language
that resonates with their feelings and values.
Effective use of pathos can make your message more memorable and impactful.
Lastly, logos is the appeal to logic and reason.
This involves presenting clear, rational arguments supported by facts, statistics, and logical reasoning.
Your aim here is to construct a compelling case that your audience can understand and accept, based
on its merit.
Now, how do we blend these elements into our public speaking?
Start with a strong opening that establishes your credibility ethos and engages your audience's emotions.
Pathos.
This could be a personal story related to your topic, a surprising statistic, or a thought provoking
question.
As you move into the body of your speech, focus on building your argument logos with clear, concise
points.
Use evidence and examples to support your claims and explain how your message aligns with your audience's
needs and values.
Remember, persuasion is not about manipulation.
It's about convincing others to consider a new perspective or take action based on genuine understanding
and agreement.
Engage with your audience throughout your speech.
Ask rhetorical questions.
Invite them to imagine scenarios, and use inclusive language to make them feel part of your narrative.
This not only keeps their attention but also strengthens your pathos appeal.
In conclusion, mastering the art of persuasion in public speaking allows you to create powerful, impactful
messages that can influence thought and action by effectively employing ethos, pathos, and logos.
You can connect with your audience on a deeper level, earn their trust, and guide them towards your
intended outcome.
Remember, the key to persuasive speaking is not just in what you say, but in how you say it and how
well you connect with your listeners.
